Apache. The southwestern Athabaskan people traditionally inhabiting Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Texas, Colorado, and Mexico. They were organized into autonomous bands and known for their skilled horsemanship, raiding traditions, and fierce resistance to U.S. and Spanish colonial domination, maintaining independence longer than most Plains and Southwestern nations.

As Athabaskan-speaking peoples distantly related to the Navajo, the Apache divided into autonomous bands including the Western Apache, Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, and others, each with their own leaders and territories. They practiced a mixed economy of hunting, gathering, agriculture, and after acquiring horses, raiding and warfare against Spanish and Mexican settlements.

One of their most famous leaders was Geronimo, known in Apache as Goyathlay. He led the Chiricahua Apache in a prolonged resistance campaign from 1876 to 1886, conducting guerrilla warfare across the Southwest and Mexico before finally surrendering. Throughout this period, the Apache were subjected to forced relocations, including the San Carlos Reservation concentration, and endured military campaigns and decimation of their buffalo hunting grounds.

Perhaps most strikingly, Apache scouts were enlisted by the U.S. Army during the Indian Wars, serving as guides and fighters in campaigns against their own people. Today six federally recognized Apache nations exist, and strong cultural traditions and language preservation efforts continue across their reservations. They share ancestry with the Navajo, another Athabaskan-speaking nation that inhabited the same Southwest homeland and experienced Spanish colonial history.
